rows.grounds: eka (single) + vijñātṛ (knower) + vedyatva (knowability); state of being knowable to one knower

items.question: If an entity's nature is object-manifestation, can it be knowable to only one knower?
premises: An entity is taken to have the nature of object-manifestation.
If such manifestation were unreal, knowability restricted to a single knower would follow.
Knowability by another knower would then be excluded.
items.inference: Restricting knowability to a single knower conflicts with the nature of manifestation as such.
uncertainties: The exact force of tvasat (unreal as hypothetical or as consequence) is slightly compressed in the verse.
items.plain_english: If an entity’s very nature were the manifestation of an object, then treating that manifestation as unreal would make it knowable only to one knower and not to any other. This shows the problem with limiting knowability to a single knower.

items.question: Can knowability be a property belonging to an entity in itself?
premises: If knowability belonged to all knowers, it could not belong to only one knower.
If it belonged to only one knower, it could not belong to all knowers.
A property that shifts with the knower cannot be an intrinsic property of the entity.
items.inference: Knowability is not any intrinsic property of an entity.
items.plain_english: If something were knowable by all knowers, it would not be knowable by only one; and the reverse also fails. Therefore, knowability is not an intrinsic property of an entity at all.

items.question: What is the knowability of an entity if it is not an intrinsic property of the entity?
premises: Knowability of an entity is identified with an arising of consciousness.
This arising takes the form of grasping an object.
Such object-grasping occurs within consciousness itself.
items.inference: An entity's knowability is nothing other than consciousness arising in the form of object-grasping.
items.plain_english: The knowability of an entity is just the arising of consciousness in the form of grasping an object. It happens within consciousness itself, not as a property sitting in the entity.

rows.grounds: prakāśya (manifest, to be illuminated) + artha (object) + tam (that)

items.question: What exactly counts as knowability in relation to a manifest object?
premises: When consciousness converges on a manifest object, that convergence is called knowability.
Knowability is thus defined from the side of consciousness, not from the side of the object.
If knowability were a property of objects, it would belong to them independently of this convergence.
items.inference: Knowability is the conscious convergence on a manifest object, not a property of objects themselves.
items.plain_english: When consciousness comes together with a manifest object, that very event is what we call knowability. So we say knowability is not a property belonging to objects.

rows.gloss: in the form of broad base and so on
rows.grounds: pṛthu (broad) + budhna (base) + ādi (and so on) + rūpa (form)

items.question: What follows if knowability were treated as a property of objects even when knowledge is present?
premises: If knowability were an object-property, objects would remain unknowable even when knowledge of them is present.
A described form present in one thing does not by itself transfer to another thing.
The pot's form, such as having a broad base, illustrates this non-transfer.
items.inference: Making knowability an object-property yields the absurd result that objects stay unknowable despite knowledge.
uncertainties: The addressee of te (they/to you) is context-dependent; taken here as 'they' (the objects).
items.plain_english: If knowability were a property of objects, they would remain unknowable even when knowledge of them is present and described. Just as a pot may have a broad base and other features, that does not by itself make something else share that form.

rows.gloss: the state of having broad-base form and so on
rows.grounds: pṛthu (broad) + budhna (base) + ādi (and so on) + rūpa (form) + -tā (state)

items.question: Does the mere presence of consciousness in a knower make objects knowable?
premises: A cloth does not acquire the pot's broad-base form merely because that form exists elsewhere.
Consciousness may be present and inhere in the knower.
A property not belonging to an object's nature cannot be transferred to it by mere presence of something else.
items.inference: Even when consciousness inheres in the knower, entities do not become knowable if knowability were an external property.
items.plain_english: A cloth does not become broad-based just because a pot is. In the same way, even if consciousness is present and belongs to the knower, entities would not become knowable if knowability were something external to them.

items.question: How could entities with an unknowable nature ever become knowable?
premises: If entities were by nature unknowable, no external factor could make them knowable.
This consequence is a very great absurdity.
The problem arises from treating the entity itself as lacking the nature of manifestation.
items.inference: Entities cannot be intrinsically unknowable and yet somehow attain knowability.
items.plain_english: If entities were unknowable by nature, how could they ever become knowable? That would be a huge absurdity, so we must look carefully at what an entity itself is.

rows.gloss: mind lamp eye and so on
rows.grounds: manas (mind) + dīpa (lamp) + cakṣus (eye) + ādi (and so on)

items.question: Can an unlit consciousness or unlit instruments account for manifestation?
premises: What is of luminous nature is not the same as an unlit consciousness.
Mind, lamp, eye, and similar instruments are themselves unlit supports.
An unlit support cannot by itself produce luminosity.
items.inference: Neither unlit consciousness nor unlit instruments can explain manifestation.
uncertainties: The syntactic break between saṃvit and aprakāśā is compact; read as contrasting luminous nature with unlit consciousness/supports.
items.plain_english: What is luminous by nature is not an unlit consciousness, nor is it something resting on unlit supports like the mind, a lamp, or the eye. Those things are unlit in the same way and cannot explain manifestation by themselves.

rows.grounds: particle introducing an objection or reminder

items.question: What does it mean for knowledge to be luminous when the world is asleep?
premises: When the whole world is asleep, ordinary manifestation is absent.
It is commonly said that knowledge's nature is to manifest objects, like a lamp.
The analogy with a lamp needs clarification in this context.
items.inference: The claim that knowledge manifests objects like a lamp requires careful analysis, especially when ordinary manifestation is absent.
uncertainties: Whether supte jagati refers to deep sleep, dissolution, or a general absence of manifestation is not fully specified here.
items.plain_english: What does it really mean for knowledge to be luminous when the whole world is asleep? People say knowledge manifests objects like a lamp, but that comparison needs to be examined.

rows.grounds: narī (woman) + nṛtyāmahe (we dance); idiomatic expression of excitement or display

items.question: What exactly is the form of knowledge's object-manifestation?
premises: Calling knowledge lamp-like is treated as no great discovery.
The key issue is to determine what object-manifestation actually is as the form of knowledge.
A mere analogy does not settle the nature of that manifestation.
items.inference: The nature of knowledge's object-manifestation must be directly analyzed rather than assumed by analogy.
uncertainties: narīnṛtyāmahe is idiomatic and may carry a mildly ironic tone; rendered literally with that sense in mind.
items.plain_english: There is nothing remarkable in simply saying we know this. What matters is to determine clearly what object-manifestation is as the very form of knowledge.

rows.gloss: if luminosity is the form, the object

items.question: What is meant when luminosity is said to be the form of object-manifestation?
premises: One option is that the object itself is luminosity.
Another option is that knowledge alone is luminosity.
A third option is that luminosity belongs to the object as its form.
items.inference: The phrase 'luminosity is its form' is ambiguous and must be disambiguated among these options.
uncertainties: The compressed syntax allows slightly different punctuations; the three-way disjunction is the clearest reading.
items.plain_english: If we say luminosity is the form involved in object-manifestation, do we mean the object is luminosity, or knowledge alone is, or that luminosity belongs to the object as its form? The expression is ambiguous and must be clarified.

items.question: How should the possessive relation in 'luminosity of the object' be grammatically understood?
premises: If the sixth case is taken in the agent sense, a serious fault follows.
If the sixth case is taken in the object sense, the causal force of the expression must be located properly.
The grammatical analysis determines the philosophical meaning of object-manifestation.
items.inference: The possessive relation cannot be read as agentive without defect; its correct reading depends on a careful object-side and causal analysis.
uncertainties: The precise technical force of ṇyartha in this compact grammatical argument may admit nuanced readings.
items.plain_english: If we take the phrase 'luminosity of the object' as meaning the object is the agent of luminosity, that leads to a serious problem. If we take it in the object sense, then we must carefully place the causal force of the expression. The grammar here matters for the philosophy.
